summary: To limit privacy problems from tying a device, its traffic, its location, and its user together, device makers use MAC address randomization, especially in Wi-Fi. This informational RFC describes that technology, how it affects networks, and the use cases involved.

eli5.summary: Your device's hardware name can be used to follow you around. Randomizing it is like wearing a different name tag in each place, which also changes how networks treat you.

questions: how does random mac affect wi-fi networks
why do devices randomize mac addresses
device tracking and privacy on wifi
subtitle: How and why devices change their hardware addresses for privacy

tldr.problem: A device's MAC address can uniquely identify it and be tracked across locations, linking the device to its user's movements and online activity, especially on Wi-Fi networks where the MAC address is broadcast in the clear.
tldr.mechanism: Device operating systems randomize and change MAC addresses to break the persistent association between a device, its traffic, and its user, making it harder for observers to track the device.
tldr.outcome: While randomization protects privacy, it disrupts network services that rely on stable MAC addresses, such as IP address assignment and device authentication. Networks and devices must balance privacy with service reliability.

today: RFC 9797 is an Informational RFC describing the current state of MAC address randomization technology. Most modern devices (smartphones, laptops, tablets) implement some form of MAC address randomization by default, though the specific behavior varies by device and operating system. Enterprise and home networks continue to adapt their services to work with randomized addresses.

sections.title: Why MAC Addresses Matter for Privacy
sections.content:
Every network device has a MAC address, a hardware-level identifier that networks use to route data to the right device. In the early days of Ethernet, this was fine—devices sat in offices and rarely moved. But wireless networks changed everything. A Wi-Fi device's MAC address broadcasts over the air with every frame it sends, and anyone with surveillance equipment in range can see it. Even more troubling, the same MAC address follows the user everywhere, allowing observers to track a specific device across locations, deduce where the person works and lives, and link all their network activity together.

This is not accidental—it is the design of IEEE 802 networks. The MAC address was meant to be a persistent, globally unique identifier. Once an observer learns that a specific MAC address belongs to a person, they can monitor that person's traffic without ever knowing their name.
sections.eli5: Your device's hardware name is unique and stays the same forever. That makes it easy for someone listening to Wi-Fi signals to follow you around and see what you do on the internet.

sections.title: MAC Address Randomization: The Solution
sections.content:
Client operating systems now implement Randomized and Changing MAC (RCM) addresses. Instead of using one fixed MAC address, a device changes to a new, random address at intervals—sometimes when joining a new Wi-Fi network, sometimes at regular time intervals, sometimes for different networks. Since the addresses are locally administered (not registered with IEEE as global identifiers), the device can create them on the fly without coordination.

The effect is powerful: an observer monitoring Wi-Fi signals can no longer easily link traffic from the same device over time or track a person's location. If the device changes its MAC address hourly or even more frequently, the attacker must do far more work to re-identify it, and the effort becomes impractical.
sections.eli5: Your device picks a new name tag randomly whenever it connects to Wi-Fi. This makes it hard for someone to recognize you as the same device in different places.

sections.title: The Network Services Problem
sections.content:
For decades, network equipment has assumed MAC addresses are stable. This assumption is embedded in dozens of services:

  • DHCP servers use MAC addresses to remember which IP address to assign to returning devices, so the device gets the same address every time it connects.
  • Access points cache encryption keys and session state by MAC address; when a MAC changes, the entire context is lost and re-authentication is needed.
  • 802.1X port security uses MAC addresses to enforce authorization rules; a new MAC address looks like a new (possibly unauthorized) device.
  • ARP tables and MAC learning tables in switches rely on the MAC-to-IP mapping staying stable during a session.
  • Parental controls and security filters in home networks are keyed to MAC addresses.
  • AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) services bind users and devices to their MAC addresses for auditing and policy enforcement.

When a device randomizes its MAC address without warning, these services break. Re-authentication takes time, users experience dropped connections, video streams pause, and real-time applications like video calls stutter. In enterprise networks, IT support becomes harder because the same device appears to be dozens of different devices in the logs.
sections.eli5: Networks and devices remember who you are by your name tag, so you get the same internet address and your home Wi-Fi knows to let you in. When you change your name tag suddenly, everything gets confused and has to re-learn who you are, which can interrupt your internet.

sections.title: Trust Levels and Design Choices
sections.content:
The RFC recognizes that the right amount of MAC randomization depends on context. In a fully trusted environment—like your home Wi-Fi under your control—you trust the access point and the people managing it. There is no eavesdropper, and the device can use a persistent MAC address without privacy loss.

In a zero-trust environment—like a coffee shop or airport hotspot—the device should randomize aggressively, changing its MAC address frequently to prevent anyone from building a profile of you.

In between are selective-trust environments, where a device might use different persistent MAC addresses for different SSIDs or different times of day. For example, in a corporate BYOD network where the IT department is trusted but external eavesdroppers are not, the device could use one stable MAC address on the internal network and change it when roaming to external networks.

The key design challenge is choosing how often to randomize: too frequently and networks break; too rarely and privacy suffers. The RFC lists five common network environments and the trade-offs in each.
sections.eli5: In a trusted place like your home, your device can keep the same name tag. At a coffee shop or airport, it should change frequently. In corporate networks, a device might keep one name tag at work and change it elsewhere.

sections.title: Frameworks for Coexistence
sections.content:
The RFC describes existing frameworks that try to preserve both privacy and network efficiency:

IEEE 802.1X with WPA2/WPA3 allows a device to authenticate using credentials that hide the password from the network, and then randomize the MAC address during disconnections and reconnections. However, re-authentication adds latency and load to the server.

OpenRoaming uses a federation approach: the device authenticates through a trusted third party rather than directly to the local network. This way, the local network operator does not learn the user's identity, and the device can safely randomize the MAC address.

Proprietary RCM schemes (implemented by OS vendors like Apple, Google, and Microsoft) allow selective randomization: the device keeps the same MAC address on trusted networks and changes it elsewhere, or changes the address at regular intervals while disconnected from the network.
sections.eli5: Some networks let your device prove it is allowed to connect without revealing who you are, so the device can change its name tag safely. Other networks remember your device when you reconnect, even with a new name tag, because you logged in with a trusted account.
